work.title: The Second Part of King Henry the Fourth
work.author: William Shakespeare

content.text: Enter Shallow, Falstaff, Bardolph and Page.

lines.text: By cock and pie, sir, you shall not away tonight.
lines.plainText: By cock and pie sir you shall not away tonight

lines.text: What, Davy, I say!
lines.plainText: What Davy I say

lines.text: You must excuse me, Master Robert Shallow.
lines.plainText: You must excuse me Master Robert Shallow

lines.text: I will not excuse you, you shall not be excused. Excuses shall not be admitted, there is no excuse shall serve, you shall not be excused. Why, Davy!
lines.plainText: I will not excuse you you shall not be excused Excuses shall not be admitted there is no excuse shall serve you shall not be excused Why Davy

lines.text: Here, sir.
lines.plainText: Here sir

lines.text: Davy, Davy, Davy, Davy, let me see, Davy, let me see, Davy, let me see. Yea, marry, William cook, bid him come hither. Sir John, you shall not be excused.
lines.plainText: Davy Davy Davy Davy let me see Davy let me see Davy let me see Yea marry William cook bid him come hither Sir John you shall not be excused

lines.text: Marry, sir, thus: those precepts cannot be served; and again, sir—shall we sow the hade land with wheat?
lines.plainText: Marry sir thus those precepts cannot be served and again sirshall we sow the hade land with wheat

lines.text: With red wheat, Davy. But for William cook, are there no young pigeons?
lines.plainText: With red wheat Davy But for William cook are there no young pigeons

lines.text: Yes, sir. Here is now the smith's note for shoeing and plough-irons.
lines.plainText: Yes sir Here is now the smith's note for shoeing and ploughirons

lines.text: Let it be cast and paid. Sir John, you shall not be excused.
lines.plainText: Let it be cast and paid Sir John you shall not be excused

lines.text: Now, sir, a new link to the bucket must needs be had. And, sir, do you mean to stop any of William's wages, about the sack he lost the other day at Hinckley fair?
lines.plainText: Now sir a new link to the bucket must needs be had And sir do you mean to stop any of William's wages about the sack he lost the other day at Hinckley fair

lines.text: He shall answer it. Some pigeons, Davy, a couple of short-legged hens, a joint of mutton, and any pretty little tiny kickshaws, tell William cook.
lines.plainText: He shall answer it Some pigeons Davy a couple of shortlegged hens a joint of mutton and any pretty little tiny kickshaws tell William cook

lines.text: Doth the man of war stay all night, sir?
lines.plainText: Doth the man of war stay all night sir

lines.text: Yea, Davy, I will use him well: a friend i' th' court is better than a penny in purse. Use his men well, Davy, for they are arrant knaves, and will backbite.
lines.plainText: Yea Davy I will use him well a friend i' th' court is better than a penny in purse Use his men well Davy for they are arrant knaves and will backbite

lines.text: No worse than they are backbitten, sir, for they have marvellous foul linen.
lines.plainText: No worse than they are backbitten sir for they have marvellous foul linen

lines.text: Well conceited, Davy. About thy business, Davy.
lines.plainText: Well conceited Davy About thy business Davy

lines.text: I beseech you, sir, to countenance William Visor of Woncot against Clement Perkes o' th' hill.
lines.plainText: I beseech you sir to countenance William Visor of Woncot against Clement Perkes o' th' hill

lines.text: There is many complaints, Davy, against that Visor. That Visor is an arrant knave, on my knowledge.
lines.plainText: There is many complaints Davy against that Visor That Visor is an arrant knave on my knowledge

lines.text: I grant your worship that he is a knave, sir, but yet, God forbid, sir, but a knave should have some countenance at his friend's request. An honest man, sir, is able to speak for himself, when a knave is not. I have served your worship truly, sir, this eight years; and if I cannot once or twice in a quarter bear out a knave against an honest man, I have but a very little credit with your worship. The knave is mine honest friend, sir; therefore I beseech your worship let him be countenanced.
lines.plainText: I grant your worship that he is a knave sir but yet God forbid sir but a knave should have some countenance at his friend's request An honest man sir is able to speak for himself when a knave is not I have served your worship truly sir this eight years and if I cannot once or twice in a quarter bear out a knave against an honest man I have but a very little credit with your worship The knave is mine honest friend sir therefore I beseech your worship let him be countenanced

lines.text: Go to; I say he shall have no wrong. Look about, Davy.
lines.plainText: Go to I say he shall have no wrong Look about Davy

lines.text: I am glad to see your worship.
lines.plainText: I am glad to see your worship

lines.text: I thank thee with all my heart, kind Master Bardolph; and welcome, my tall fellow [to the Page]. Come, Sir John.
lines.plainText: I thank thee with all my heart kind Master Bardolph and welcome my tall fellow to the Page Come Sir John

lines.text: I'll follow you, good Master Robert Shallow.
lines.plainText: I'll follow you good Master Robert Shallow

lines.text: [Within.] Sir John!
lines.plainText: Within Sir John

lines.text: I come, Master Shallow, I come, Master Shallow.
lines.plainText: I come Master Shallow I come Master Shallow
